Green Hydrogen’s Water Problem Is a Qualification Problem

The green-hydrogen industry is not primarily waiting for water. It is waiting for cheap electricity, reliable offtake, subsidy eligibility, grid connections, credible electrolyzer suppliers, and final investment decisions.

By Bottleneck Briefs · Published 2026-07-02 · 17 min read

In brief

  • 9 kg/kg H2 | chemical water floor before treatment, cooling, and reject losses
  • 120 MWe | Humber startup still depends on resolving an estuary-discharge condition
  • 200 MW | Holland Hydrogen 1 will test packaged ultrapure-water commissioning
  • 2026–2029 | first window for operating evidence on water-loop cost and reliability
  • 10 plants | clean operating sample that would materially weaken the thesis

The hidden gate appears after the visible ones

Source-document visual

Northfleet permit decision pages showing water-use challenge, purification reject, and conductivity requirement

The clearest project-level evidence: a regulator challenged the applicant’s water ratio and required a documented purification balance for a 15 MWe PEM hydrogen plant.

Open source visual from Environment Agency / GOV.UK

Reuse: UK government document; Open Government Licence likely but page-level reuse not rechecked · Attribution: Environment Agency / GOV.UK

Only after a project clears those gates does a less visible problem become important: the plant must continuously produce water that meets the electrolyzer manufacturer’s specification, prove that quality during commissioning and operation, and secure a lawful route for reverse-osmosis reject, purge water, spent media, and other residuals.

That makes feedwater a sequential constraint. It is unlikely to determine whether the global hydrogen economy scales. It can still delay an individual plant between equipment delivery and permission to operate.

The engineering processes are established. Reverse osmosis, electrodeionization, mixed-bed ion exchange, ultraviolet treatment, online conductivity monitoring, and laboratory analysis are standard industrial-water tools. The difficulty lies in connecting them across several organizations: the electrolyzer OEM, water integrator, operator, sewer or outfall owner, accredited laboratory, industrial customer, and environmental regulator.

Source-document visual

Official guidance frames water as supply, treatment, purge, wastewater, residuals, and monitoring rather than only feedstock volume.

Each party controls a different part of the evidence. The OEM controls stack acceptance and warranty conditions. The water vendor controls treatment design. The operator controls maintenance and records. The utility or outfall owner controls the residual route. The regulator controls permission to discharge and operate.

The thesis therefore survives only in a narrow form: ultrapure-water equipment is not scarce, but the certified feedwater-and-residual loop can become a project-specific commissioning and compliance gate. The stronger claim—that it is already a fleetwide O&M bottleneck or large standalone profit pool—does not yet hold.

Northfleet shows how a small loop enters the permit process

The Northfleet Hydrogen Production Facility in Gravesend, England, is the clearest documented example.

Green Hydrogen 3 received an environmental permit in February 2025 for a 15 MWe plant comprising six 2.5 MWe PEM units. The facility is designed to produce as much as 280 kilograms of hydrogen per hour and send it by dedicated pipeline to the adjacent Northfleet Paper Mill.

The applicant initially reported 4.2 cubic metres per hour of demineralized water for 280 kilograms per hour of hydrogen. The Environment Agency challenged that figure against the roughly 9:1 chemical minimum.

The manufacturer then separated the flows into 3,456 litres per hour of incoming water, 864 litres per hour removed in purification, and 2,592 litres per hour consumed as pure water. The disclosed rounded numbers imply approximately 9.3 kilograms of pure water per kilogram of hydrogen. The regulator’s narrative described the result as approximately 9.1.

The same decision document specified feedwater conductivity below 1 microsiemens per centimetre and recorded that reverse-osmosis effluent would enter the foul sewer under a Southern Water trade-effluent consent. (Environment Agency Northfleet decision document)

The significance is not that Northfleet consumes an extraordinary amount of water. It does not. The significance is that an apparently minor balance-of-plant subsystem became part of the regulator’s evidence chain.

Northfleet also illustrates a second coordination problem. Producing hydrogen is insufficient unless the customer’s equipment is ready to consume it. Kimberly-Clark subsequently applied to vary the paper mill’s environmental permit for hydrogen-capable replacement boilers. The producer and customer therefore have separate construction, commissioning, and regulatory clocks.

This is the type of interface that project models often compress into a single “commissioning” date. In practice, the plant, pipeline, boiler, water-treatment system, discharge route, and permit conditions must all close together.

Humber turns feedwater into receiving-water risk

Uniper’s Humber H2ub Green project makes the same mechanism larger.

The proposed first phase at Killingholme would install six 20 MW ITM Power PEM modules, creating 120 MWe of electrolysis capacity. Planning documents describe roughly 21,000 normal cubic metres of hydrogen per hour, supply to Phillips 66’s Humber Refinery, and potential expansion beyond 200 MWe.

The project considered refinery effluent, other industrial effluent, and non-potable water as possible sources. It also selected air cooling partly because water supply on the South Humber Bank is constrained.

Those choices show that water affects design before it affects operations. A developer may avoid evaporative cooling, accept a higher electricity burden, or build additional pretreatment to reduce dependence on scarce potable supply.

The sharper issue is the discharge route. The proposed water-treatment plant would send wastewater and site drainage through the existing KPS-B outfall into the Humber Estuary.

The planning condition states that operation cannot begin until the authority receives either an environmental permit establishing water-borne pollutant limits agreed with the Environment Agency and Natural England, or confirmation that the protected estuary’s conservation objectives will not be compromised. (North Lincolnshire planning report)

This is a genuine operating gate. Yet it should not be confused with the project’s primary commercial gate.

Uniper’s current indicative schedule places front-end engineering in 2026, final investment decision in 2027, and commercial operation in 2030. Electricity economics, public support, refinery demand, contracting, and finance must converge before the discharge condition becomes the last unresolved item.

Water matters because the project advanced far enough for it to matter.

Figures come from project owners, regulators, planning authorities, suppliers, and the IEA.

The comparison shows why one label does not fit the entire sector.

Northfleet and Humber provide strong permit evidence but little operating evidence. Holland Hydrogen 1 provides procurement and near-term commissioning evidence. Orica provides a funded industrial-use case but has not yet qualified its water system in operation. Kuqa and Puertollano provide counterexamples: substantial electrolyzer plants can operate without feedwater becoming the publicly visible problem.

NEOM is the scale test. The project combines more than 2 GW of alkaline electrolysis with green-ammonia production and export infrastructure. A coastal desert site naturally raises questions about desalination, marine discharge, and brine. Yet the captured public record does not establish that those issues are pacing the project.

The more visible NEOM risks are power construction, electrolyzer installation, ammonia synthesis, export logistics, finance, and integrated commissioning. A claim that feedwater is binding there would require project-specific desalination contracts, environmental assessments, marine permits, or operating records—not an inference from the surrounding desert.

Orica shows that commercial bankability comes first

Orica’s Hunter Valley Hydrogen Hub is the strongest counterweight to a water-centric interpretation.

The company reached final investment decision on 1 July 2026 for a 50 MW first phase at Kooragang Island near Newcastle. The project is expected to produce approximately 4,700 tonnes of renewable hydrogen and 26,600 tonnes of low-carbon ammonia per year, reducing natural-gas feedstock use in Orica’s existing ammonia operations.

Recycled water is embedded in the design. It should not yet be described as operationally “solved,” because the project has not started producing hydrogen.

The observed development history nevertheless points elsewhere. Origin Energy exited the earlier project structure in October 2024, citing slow hydrogen-market development and capital-intensive risk. Orica later proceeded with captive industrial demand and a substantial support stack, including AUD 432 million of performance-linked Hydrogen Headstart credits. (Orica FID)

The economic sequence is clear. The project required a customer, an industrial integration case, public support, and an acceptable allocation of capital risk before its recycled-water configuration became relevant to construction.

This pattern is consistent with the broader hydrogen market. Announced pipelines remain much larger than committed projects. High electricity costs, uncertain demand, infrastructure gaps, and policy execution continue to remove or delay projects before detailed feedwater qualification can become critical.

The most accurate hierarchy is therefore:

1. Commercial bankability determines whether the project advances. 2. Equipment and construction determine whether it reaches commissioning. 3. Feedwater qualification and residual permission can determine whether it passes acceptance and begins stable operation.

Packaging is arriving faster than scarcity

Holland Hydrogen 1 provides evidence that industrial suppliers can package the water problem.

Shell’s Rotterdam project uses a 200 MW thyssenkrupp nucera electrolyzer system and is designed to produce around 60 tonnes of hydrogen per day. Pure Water Group says nucera selected it to supply the ultrapure-water generation package.

Shell’s current schedule calls for commissioning in late 2026 and production ramp-up in 2027. An older supplier claim that the plant would be fully operational in 2025 is stale. (Shell hydrogen projects)

The supplier selection matters because it places the water package inside the electrolyzer supply chain. The OEM can approve the treatment design, align acceptance requirements, and reduce the number of interfaces presented to the owner.

Veolia already markets standard systems for projects in the 20–100 MW range and bespoke configurations above 500 MW. DuPont, Ecolab’s Purolite, and LANXESS offer ion-exchange media aimed at electrolyzer makeup water or PEM recirculation loops. Xylem’s Evoqua operations provide portable deionization, off-site resin regeneration, laboratory support, and emergency mobile treatment.

Purolite markets a target above 18 megohm-centimetres for PEM recirculating-loop water. That is a vendor-specific loop target, not a universal commercial feedwater standard. Independent literature more commonly describes manufacturer feedwater requirements around less than 1 microsiemens per centimetre, with specifications varying by OEM and measurement point.

The relief picture is therefore already visible. Treatment equipment and media exist. No hydrogen-specific shortage or vendor backlog has been demonstrated.

The period from 2026 through 2029 will test whether these packages merely arrive on site or pass acceptance routinely under variable source water, intermittent operation, and real residual-discharge conditions.

Where spending could move—and where it may not

If the mechanism becomes repeatable, water-related spending should divide into three categories.

The first is initial capital: pretreatment, RO or CEDI, polishing, storage tanks, analyzers, controls, and residual-handling equipment. This is likely to remain bundled through the EPC contractor, electrolyzer OEM, or water integrator.

The second is qualification spending: factory acceptance testing, site acceptance testing, laboratory campaigns, calibration, regulator submissions, customer-side permit changes, and commissioning contingencies.

The third is recurring service: resin replacement, vessel exchange, off-site regeneration, membrane maintenance, analyzer calibration, sampling, mobile-water backup, and wastewater compliance.

The third category is the most interesting commercially, but it is also the least proven.

Xylem already offers fixed-period service deionization, regeneration, exchange vessels, and emergency dispatch in conventional industrial markets. Ecolab acquired Purolite partly for a purification business dominated by consumable products. DuPont and LANXESS sell application-specific resins.

None of that establishes hydrogen-specific revenue. The same systems serve power plants, pharmaceutical facilities, semiconductor fabs, refineries, and general industry. Hydrogen may become an incremental application rather than a distinct high-margin market.

The electrolyzer OEM may also retain most of the bargaining power. If the water skid is bundled inside a larger package, the component supplier’s revenue may be pass-through content rather than a separate profit pool. Public subsidies support the project owner; they are not water-vendor sales. Announced megawatts are not booked revenue.

The current evidence supports a map of potential control points, not a claim that abnormal margins have migrated to them.

The closest base rate is ordinary industrial water

The closest historical precedent is not a hydrogen boom. It is the long development of demineralized-water service in power generation, refining, chemicals, and other process industries.

Those sectors built mature networks for ion-exchange media, portable DI vessels, off-site regeneration, membrane cleaning, sampling, laboratory analysis, and emergency response. Water quality became a recurring operating discipline without creating a permanent shortage of purification equipment.

Green hydrogen is similar because electrochemical equipment requires controlled water chemistry, validated treatment, and residual handling.

It is different because the electrolyzer fleet is younger, OEM specifications are less standardized, renewable-power operation is more variable, and many projects still depend on public support and unproven demand.

Semiconductor fabrication offers a second analogy. Fabs turned ultrapure water, recycling, and reclaimed-water infrastructure into strategic site-selection issues. But semiconductor facilities generally use much larger water systems and face more demanding purity requirements. That precedent demonstrates how water can influence industrial location and resilience; it does not establish the same economics for hydrogen.

The base rate points toward gradual standardization. Basic equipment becomes routine. Value, where it persists, tends to sit in integration, local service capacity, monitoring, contingency response, and permission to discharge.

The strongest evidence against the thesis

A credible article must account for operating plants that do not fit the proposed problem.

China’s Kuqa project entered full operation in August 2023 at roughly 260 MW equivalent. A later public update reported 335 days of safe and steady operation. The prominent technical problem was renewable-power variability and electrolyzer control, not feedwater treatment or residual handling. (Kuqa operating update)

Iberdrola’s 20 MW Puertollano plant has operated since 2022. Its public narrative centres on renewable electricity and fertilizer production rather than an unusual water constraint. (Puertollano project)

These cases do not prove that water-loop problems never occur. Public operating disclosure is incomplete, and smaller or state-backed projects may not publish detailed maintenance information.

They do show that feedwater is not automatically the dominant operating problem. A fleetwide claim would require disclosed outages, warranty disputes, persistent resin consumption, unusual service costs, or repeated commissioning failures. The current record contains none of those at meaningful scale.

The thesis should be considered disproven if ten 50 MW-or-larger projects complete two full operating years without material feedwater-related acceptance failures, downtime, warranty disputes, residual interventions, or separately visible service costs.

What to watch

  • 2026-12-31: Shell reports whether Holland Hydrogen 1 has formally entered commissioning.
  • 2027-12-31: Shell reports first hydrogen production or a revised Holland Hydrogen 1 schedule.
  • 2027-12-31: Uniper announces Humber H2ub Green FID and the status of its discharge condition.
  • 2029-06-30: Orica reports first renewable-hydrogen production at Kooragang Island.
  • 2030-12-31: A second 50 MW-plus project receives a binding residual-discharge startup condition.
  • 2031-12-31: An operating 50 MW-plus project discloses a quantified water-loop O&M metric.

The conclusion depends on operating records

Green hydrogen does not face a global shortage of water-treatment technology. Industrial suppliers already know how to produce deionized and ultrapure water. They know how to regenerate resin, maintain membranes, deploy mobile equipment, and monitor effluent.

The unresolved issue is whether first-generation 50–200 MW projects can make those capabilities routine across fragmented contracts and regulators.

Northfleet proves that water arithmetic and sewer routing can enter a permit decision. Humber proves that receiving-water protection can remain an explicit pre-operation condition. Holland Hydrogen 1 proves that a large UPW package can be integrated into an electrolyzer supply chain. Orica proves that commercial support and industrial demand usually come first. Kuqa and Puertollano show that plants can operate without water becoming the publicly visible constraint.

The likely outcome is neither a global bottleneck nor a non-issue. Feedwater becomes one more chemical-plant discipline: usually manageable, occasionally critical, and most dangerous when owners treat it as a minor package until late in the project.

The next decisive evidence will not come from another resin launch or capacity announcement. It will come from commissioning records, warranty terms, discharge permits, service contracts, replacement intervals, and documented downtime.

Until those records arrive, the defensible claim is limited but useful: green hydrogen’s water problem is not finding water. It is proving that each site can keep the water loop within specification and the residual stream within the law.
